Eddie Possehl is a dynamic and driven writer/director with a passion for the written word and all things film, television, comics, and games. His passion for storytelling led him to establish his own production company in hopes of achieving his dreams.
His dedication to his craft has attracted renowned talent like Yuri Lowenthal to collaborate with him on his projects. As he grows and improves, Eddie is a shining example of a self-starter.

Sure, it's one thing to make one good superhero movie — that's challenging enough as it is. However, when it comes to major franchises, the movies never stop at the first release; most studios opt for the trilogy format for their series. Over the many decades that superhero films have reigned over cinema, there have been numerous trilogies that have hit screens.

Making a trilogy isn't easy — not in the slightest — thanks to how important a good batting average for one needs to be. People will be hard-pressed to find a superhero trilogy where every single movie is astounding. At the end of the day, though, just the majority of them need to be amazing, and that alone can result in a good trilogy of projects. Which ones are the best, though? It's a tough competition, but there are definitely some that rise above the others.

8
Deadpool's Raunchy Trilogy
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/mcddean_wd032-1.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Hugh Jackman and Ryan Reynolds in 'Deadpool & Wolverine'

blocks.x: Image via Jay Maidment /© Marvel / © Walt Disney Studios Motion Pictures / Courtesy Everett Collection

After the first Deadpool movie came out all the way back in 2016, people were clamoring for more. From that moment onward, it was pretty much written in the stars that Ryan Reynolds' new hit series was going to get more projects. It sparked an R-rated superhero series unlike any other. Just two years later, Deadpool 2 came out, and while it wasn't the perfect project, it still had the humor and gory action that made the first entry so successful in the first place.

The biggest of the three — at least financially — is the most recent third movie, Deadpool & Wolverine, released in 2024. Not only is this an all-around funny and action-packed production, but it made a huge mark by being the first X-Men-related Fox property to debut in the Marvel Cinematic Universe. It brought back the likes of Wesley Snipes as Blade, Chris Evans as Johnny Storm, Jennifer Garner as Elektra, and, of course, Hugh Jackman as Wolverine (a crossover that everyone had been asking for). With how impactful the Deadpool series has been — giving new life to R-rated superhero movies — it has earned its spot among the best.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F64c40d5debd38-Screenshot%202022-10-19%20141001.png?fit=crop&w=90&h=90

7
Iron Man's High-Flying Trilogy
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/robert-downey-jr-tony-stark-iron-man-1.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Robert Downey Jr as Tony Stark holding up robotic hand in Iron Man (2008)

blocks.x: Image via Marvel Studios

The trilogy that started it all, making the MCU possible in the first place, is unforgettable. The first Iron Man is commonly known as one of the best superhero movies of all time, and the following flicks, while not having the same renown, each have a lot to love about them. The most infamous of the three, Iron Man 2, may have gotten a lot of flak over the years, but the weakest of the trilogy actually comes in the form of Iron Man 3, which struggled to keep things engaging — just a little bit. But it was massively appreciated for the way it delved deeper into the psyche of Tony Stark (Robert Downey Jr.), which made up for the lack of actual Iron Man in the runtime.

As stated, though, many have consistently claimed that Iron Man 2 is the weakest, but in hindsight, it is a lot better than many give it credit for (especially after what was just the weakest age of the MCU). Before the cinematic universe started truly getting the criticism about each project feeling same-y, Iron Man 2 held the directorial vision of Jon Favreau and still holds a plethora of identity. Not to mention, much like Iron Man, the visual effects here hold up against and even outweigh a lot of the modern VFX in modern MCU projects. This is thanks to Favreau deciding to always use a practical Iron Man armor (typically a half-body one) to enhance the look of the armor in the movie.

6
X-Men's E(X)cellent Trilogy
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/x2-x-men-united.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: The X-Men standing in a darkly-lit room and looking directly at the camera in X2.

blocks.x: Image via 20th Century Studios

Yes, the third movie of this trilogy, X-Men: The Last Stand, is considered one of the worst superhero movies of all time. However, this is made far more bearable by the fact that the first two projects in this series are phenomenal. Many trilogies typically have an excellent, a good, and a mid-tier to bad entry. However, the structure of the X-Men series is excellent, even better, and then terrible. That's a pretty good batting average for a superhero trilogy, especially from the early 2000s.

The X-Men have always been some of the most important Marvel Comics characters of all time, and this trilogy is a huge reason casual cinema-goers grew to love them so much. This series handles the typical topics of discrimination and bigotry that this team's stories usually do with grace, engrossment, and spectacle. X2: X-Men United is especially amazing — the best of the three projects.

Four teams, four completely different reasons to put yourself in danger

Marvel Studios · The Avengers · Since 2012
The Avengers

You belong where the stakes are largest and the personalities are
loudest. This is a team of people who are all used to being the most important person in the
room, which is exactly why it works and exactly why it keeps nearly falling apart.

The Avengers are not friends who became a team. They are a team that slowly and
reluctantly became friends, and you would recognise every stage of that process.

You can hold your own among big egos without needing to win every exchange, which is the

usually at volume, usually in a very expensive building.

The X-Men

You have never had the luxury of being thanked for this. The
X-Men protect a world that has never once been comfortable with them existing, and something
in you understands exactly why they keep doing it anyway.

This is the only team on the list whose central conflict is not a villain. It is being
wanted gone by the same people they keep saving.

You know what it is to be the outsider in a room and to decide, anyway, that you will
not make yourself smaller so everyone else is comfortable.

The X-Men are the most genuine found family in comics. People arrive with nowhere else

The Teen Titans

You do not want colleagues, you want your people. The Titans are
the team where the friendship came first and the world-saving turned up afterwards as an

5
Tom Holland's Terrific Spider-Man Trilogy
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/sharedimages/2025/12/spider-man-homecoming.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Spider-Man with the US flag waving behind him in Spider-Man: Homecoming

blocks.x: Image via Sony Pictures Releasing

Particularly after Spider-Man: Brand New Day — not counting in the "home" trilogy, as it's a new director and a new era for the character, dropping the "home" naming convention — Tom Holland is many people's favorite Spider-Man. This opinion was a popular one prior to the newest masterclass of a movie, though. Holland's original Spidey trilogy, commonly called the "Home Trilogy," is beloved by many. Spider-Man: Homecoming, specifically, is noted and feels the most like a Jon Watts movie.

Thanks to Act Two being a slog, Spider-Man: Far From Home may be the weakest of the three films, but it also has two amazing acts and features one of the greatest Spider-Man movie villains of all time. Jake Gyllenhaal's Mysterio is memorable in every definition of the word. The trilogy-capper, Spider-Man: No Way Home, is the most noted of them, however, thanks to the fact that it brought back almost all of the villains from the past two Spider-Man cinema franchises (Act Three eventually including the other two Spider-Men, too). The project is well-written, and that, combined with these multiversal inclusions, has made it one of the highest-grossing superhero movies of all time. Holland's performance across all the projects is invariably phenomenal, and he acts as the shining star not just in these movies, but in the entire MCU.

4
Sam Raimi's Spectacular Spider-Man Trilogy
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/10/tobey-maguire-in-spider-man-2-1.jpg?q=49&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=2
blocks.c: Tobey Maguire with his Spider-Man mask off looking at his hands in Spider-Man 2.

blocks.x: Image via Sony Pictures Releasing

Sam Raimi's Spider-Man trilogy is one that has gone down as one of the best out there. A lot of this is because the first sequel, Spider-Man 2, is claimed to be not just one of the greatest superhero flicks of all time, but one of the best film sequels ever made, too. The first Spider-Man is about as close to an adaptation of the Stan Lee and John Romita Sr. era as they come.

Now, while Spider-Man 3 is given a lot of smack because of how cluttered and messy it can be, it, like Iron Man 2, is not given nearly enough credit. Spider-Man 3 is genuinely a lot better than many claim it is (reasoning can be found here). In all honesty, the first two acts of the film are very solid and a worthy successor to the first two movies. The rough patch just comes in Act Three, which reflects the trilogy's reception pretty well, actually. Go figure.

3
The Dark Knight's Knockout Trilogy
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/dark-knight-joker-heath-ledger-1.jpeg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Heath Ledger as The Joker in The Dark Knight

blocks.x: Image via Warner Bros.

Christopher Nolan is an incredible filmmaker, if his newest hit, The Odyssey, isn't already proof of that. The superhero fandom knows him best for his iconic Batman trilogy that began with 2005's Batman Begins. Most often known as The Dark Knight trilogy, these three films are exceptional, with the second one being one of the best superhero movies ever made and an incredible sequel film (much like Spider-Man 2).

The Dark Knight trilogy is amazing, only truly faltering in the third film, The Dark Knight Rises. While the movie is good, going from The Dark Knight to The Dark Knight Rises was a stark change that many people didn't appreciate. It just couldn't capture the same magic. That doesn't stop the first two projects from being exceptional, though, and that gives this trilogy a great batting average.

2
Captain America's Admirable Trilogy
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/05/captain-america-civil-war-chris-evans-robert-downey-jr.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: Captain America and Iron Man are face to face in Captain America: Civil War

blocks.x: Image via Marvel Studios

The Captain America trilogy is one that consistently changes the game and alters its style in a way that doesn't feel jarring, but fitting for the overall character that Captain America (Chris Evans) goes through. The first film, Captain America: The First Avenger, is bombastic, colorful, and almost whimsical, being the origin of such a hopeful character. However, when things get harder for him once he's in the modern day, Captain America: The Winter Soldier brings the character into a political thriller rather than a period piece.

From there, the third film, Captain America: Civil War, becomes far more of a larger spectacle as Steve Rogers goes against the world itself to protect his friend, Bucky Barnes (Sebastian Stan) — the relationship at the heart of the entire trilogy. Because of this, it's considered more of an "Avengers 2.5," featuring most of the main Marvel cast at the time. The series definitely ends on a high note with this one, and it was consistently good the entire way through — none of the movies are considered "bad."
https://static0.colliderimages.com/assets/images/sr-db-logo-icon-colored-dark.svg?v=1.9

1
The Guardians' Glorious Trilogy
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/guardians-holding-power-stone-together.jpg?q=70&fit=crop&w=825&dpr=1
blocks.c: The Guardians holding the Power Stone together in Guardians of the Galaxy

blocks.x: Image via Marvel Studios

One of the best superhero trilogies out there is one that's not only a space opera, but a deep, emotional journey about sharing pain with others and found family. The Guardians of the Galaxy series, brought to life by James Gunn, is so different from the rest of the MCU — and modern superhero movies in general — in all the best ways.

The humor, bright colors, and spectacle-filled space action are perfectly balanced with deep, thought-provoking messages and themes. The character arcs for each of the main cast members are well-thought-out and written with grace. The ability to balance tone is an extremely hard one to master, and Gunn proves in The Guardians of the Galaxy series that he most certainly can do it.

The Boys have no powers, no mandate and no funding. What they have is leverage,
patience, and a very high tolerance for consequences.

You are the person in the room who notices the thing everybody else has quietly agreed
not to mention.

This is not a heroic team and it has never pretended otherwise. It is a group of damaged
people doing necessary work in ways nobody would call clean.

You would not sleep well. You would keep going anyway.

5
Tom Holland's Terrific Spider-Man Trilogy

Image via Sony Pictures Releasing

Particularly after Spider-Man: Brand New Day — not counting in the "home" trilogy, as it's a new director and a new era for the character, dropping the "home" naming convention — Tom Holland is many people's favorite Spider-Man. This opinion was a popular one prior to the newest masterclass of a movie, though. Holland's original Spidey trilogy, commonly called the "Home Trilogy," is beloved by many. Spider-Man: Homecoming, specifically, is noted and feels the most like a Jon Watts movie.

Thanks to Act Two being a slog, Spider-Man: Far From Home may be the weakest of the three films, but it also has two amazing acts and features one of the greatest Spider-Man movie villains of all time. Jake Gyllenhaal's Mysterio is memorable in every definition of the word. The trilogy-capper, Spider-Man: No Way Home, is the most noted of them, however, thanks to the fact that it brought back almost all of the villains from the past two Spider-Man cinema franchises (Act Three eventually including the other two Spider-Men, too). The project is well-written, and that, combined with these multiversal inclusions, has made it one of the highest-grossing superhero movies of all time. Holland's performance across all the projects is invariably phenomenal, and he acts as the shining star not just in these movies, but in the entire MCU.

4
Sam Raimi's Spectacular Spider-Man Trilogy

Image via Sony Pictures Releasing

Sam Raimi's Spider-Man trilogy is one that has gone down as one of the best out there. A lot of this is because the first sequel, Spider-Man 2, is claimed to be not just one of the greatest superhero flicks of all time, but one of the best film sequels ever made, too. The first Spider-Man is about as close to an adaptation of the Stan Lee and John Romita Sr. era as they come.

Now, while Spider-Man 3 is given a lot of smack because of how cluttered and messy it can be, it, like Iron Man 2, is not given nearly enough credit. Spider-Man 3 is genuinely a lot better than many claim it is (reasoning can be found here). In all honesty, the first two acts of the film are very solid and a worthy successor to the first two movies. The rough patch just comes in Act Three, which reflects the trilogy's reception pretty well, actually. Go figure.

3
The Dark Knight's Knockout Trilogy

Image via Warner Bros.

Christopher Nolan is an incredible filmmaker, if his newest hit, The Odyssey, isn't already proof of that. The superhero fandom knows him best for his iconic Batman trilogy that began with 2005's Batman Begins. Most often known as The Dark Knight trilogy, these three films are exceptional, with the second one being one of the best superhero movies ever made and an incredible sequel film (much like Spider-Man 2).

The Dark Knight trilogy is amazing, only truly faltering in the third film, The Dark Knight Rises. While the movie is good, going from The Dark Knight to The Dark Knight Rises was a stark change that many people didn't appreciate. It just couldn't capture the same magic. That doesn't stop the first two projects from being exceptional, though, and that gives this trilogy a great batting average.

2
Captain America's Admirable Trilogy

Image via Marvel Studios

The Captain America trilogy is one that consistently changes the game and alters its style in a way that doesn't feel jarring, but fitting for the overall character that Captain America (Chris Evans) goes through. The first film, Captain America: The First Avenger, is bombastic, colorful, and almost whimsical, being the origin of such a hopeful character. However, when things get harder for him once he's in the modern day, Captain America: The Winter Soldier brings the character into a political thriller rather than a period piece.

From there, the third film, Captain America: Civil War, becomes far more of a larger spectacle as Steve Rogers goes against the world itself to protect his friend, Bucky Barnes (Sebastian Stan) — the relationship at the heart of the entire trilogy. Because of this, it's considered more of an "Avengers 2.5," featuring most of the main Marvel cast at the time. The series definitely ends on a high note with this one, and it was consistently good the entire way through — none of the movies are considered "bad."

1
The Guardians' Glorious Trilogy

Image via Marvel Studios

One of the best superhero trilogies out there is one that's not only a space opera, but a deep, emotional journey about sharing pain with others and found family. The Guardians of the Galaxy series, brought to life by James Gunn, is so different from the rest of the MCU — and modern superhero movies in general — in all the best ways.

The humor, bright colors, and spectacle-filled space action are perfectly balanced with deep, thought-provoking messages and themes. The character arcs for each of the main cast members are well-thought-out and written with grace. The ability to balance tone is an extremely hard one to master, and Gunn proves in The Guardians of the Galaxy series that he most certainly can do it.
